failure_modes.description: The assumption that neighboring intersections share sufficient information is fundamentally flawed. Real-world intersections have varying information quality, some may have broken sensors, and others may deliberately withhold data due to privacy concerns.
failure_modes.evidence: Studies show 15-30% of traffic sensors in urban environments fail or provide inaccurate data, making distributed optimization unreliable.

failure_modes.description: Contradicts established traffic engineering principles which show that centralized control outperforms distributed approaches for large networks due to the need for global optimization.
failure_modes.evidence: Transportation Research Board reports consistently demonstrate that centrally coordinated signal systems achieve 10-20% better throughput than distributed systems in networks with more than 10 intersections.

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis breaks at network boundaries where intersections have different communication capabilities, creating information asymmetry that prevents proper optimization.
failure_modes.evidence: Urban environments have heterogeneous infrastructure - some intersections have high-bandwidth communication while others rely on outdated systems, creating unequal information access.

failure_modes.description: The core concept is not novel - similar distributed approaches have been attempted and failed repeatedly since the 1980s.
failure_modes.evidence: Multiple peer-reviewed papers from IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems document failures of distributed signal coordination systems in real-world implementations.

failure_modes.description: The provided falsifier is actually the expected outcome - increased communication will inevitably lead to slower adaptation times and higher computational overhead without proportional benefits.
failure_modes.evidence: Computational complexity of distributed optimization grows exponentially with network size, making it impractical for real-world traffic networks with hundreds or thousands of intersections.

failure_modes.description: The slime mold analogy is fundamentally incompatible with traffic systems due to biological vs engineered system differences in response time, communication constraints, and optimization objectives.
failure_modes.evidence: Biological systems operate on completely different timescales and have evolved over millions of years, unlike engineered systems with fixed requirements and constraints.
